still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month, and almost nobody pays it.
The FDA has still approved no generic semaglutide or tirzepatide in the US, and generic liraglutide is still the only generic incretin on the US market.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and oral Wegovy starting doses still cost $149 a month there. The supply shock raised maintenance and injectable prices but not the starter price.
Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly are still the only sellers of branded incretins in the US, and Lilly still leads on efficacy.
The 503B compounding exclusion finalised in 2026 still stands, and the suicidal-ideation warning is still off the Wegovy, Zepbound and Saxenda labels.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Arithmetic: 26.5% ever-used minus 19.8% current leaves 6.7% of adults who used a drug and are off it now. 43% of ever-users have cycled, which is 11.4 points: ~9.7 points are current users on at least their second course (49% of current users) and ~1.7 points cycled before and are off again. That is consistent with roughly one-third persistence at one year and 36–47% restarting within a year. Cycling rose slightly because the 2029 price rise pushed some users into drug holidays. About 19.8% of ~268M adults is ~53M current users. FICTIONAL payer mix: commercial ~31% (~16.4M, of whom ~3.4M are in adherence-verified metabolic tracks), Medicare ~19% (~10.1M, mostly diabetes, cardiovascular and kidney codes, plus ~1.4M on the dementia-risk route), Medicaid ~7% (~3.7M in the 9 remaining opt-in states plus diabetes coverage everywhere), legitimate cash ~37% (~19.6M), imported or counterfeit ~6% (~3.2M). Payer structure is unchanged. Growth came through cash channels, mainly AUD telehealth (~4.1M adults whose primary indication is alcohol, on-label or off-label) and Foundayo maintenance switches. Under 50, the AUD route skews male and younger, which lifted the 18–29 rate from 9% to 12%. Adult obesity is ~33.9%. About 23% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, mostly uninsured, on Medicaid in non-covering states, or older adults priced out. Under-18 users number ~0.95M (1.3% of ~73M), of whom ~90k are aged 6–11. Upper-income households account for about half of pediatric use.

access.public_coverage: Coverage structure is unchanged from 2028. Medicare covers incretins under diabetes, cardiovascular, CKD and sleep-apnoea codes, and through the dementia-risk route opened Aug 2028 under prior authorisation. That route has ~1.4M beneficiaries at an estimated net ~$480/month: 1.4M × $480 × 12 ≈ $8.1B annualised. There is still no Part D weight-management benefit. Medicaid: 9 of the original 14 opt-in states still cover weight management at the $245 rate; two of them tie continued coverage to adherence and BMI progress. The 2029 supply allocation did not change Medicaid or Medicare formularies, but plans steered new starts toward Foundayo and injectables.
access.generic_rest_of_world: About 170 countries have generic semaglutide. Indian generics run $8–45/month, up slightly after India's CDSCO tightened export licensing following the 2028 US contamination case. Chinese peptide API is the volume source for most generic makers. Canada's generics are CAD 75–115.
access.note: FICTIONAL. The price shock is the May 2029 FDA warning letter at Novo's Clayton, NC semaglutide API site. Oral semaglutide at 25 mg daily uses roughly 70 times the peptide of a 2.4 mg weekly injection, so oral parity had made API capacity the binding constraint. With Clayton lots on hold, Novo put the Wegovy pill 25 mg on allocation for eleven months. Novo raised the TrumpRx maintenance price from $299 to $399 and injectable Wegovy to $449–549, and Lilly followed on Zepbound vials ($399–549). The starter price of $149 was kept. Foundayo, a small molecule unaffected by peptide supply, held at $149–349 and took share. US mail-order gray-market prices rose from ~$60–120 to ~$110–200 a month because of export tightening and CBP seizures. Users held at ~3.2M as some cash users moved down into the gray market and others moved out of it into Foundayo. Orals now make up ~58% of all users and ~70% of new starts. Employer coverage is 43% (Business Group on Health 2030), with another ~9% covering only through monitored tracks. Pharmacy trend was ~+10% in 2029.

drugs.pipeline_note: The oral_parity driver is realised within the approval rules as a new label for an existing product. In Sep 2029 the FDA added maintenance after tirzepatide induction to Foundayo's label. That followed a 52-week switch trial in which patients moved from Zepbound to orforglipron kept all but ~1.5 points of their loss (no significant difference from staying on Zepbound for maintenance). So a pill now matches the strongest injectable for maintenance but not for induction. No oral induces tirzepatide-level loss. The new_indications driver came through sNDAs Novo filed in Dec 2028. The 6–11 injectable approval came in Jan 2030, 13 months after filing; the AUD indication for oral semaglutide came in Mar 2030, 15 months after filing. Retatrutide was approved in Mar 2029 after its extended review, with dysesthesia labelling and a cap at 9 mg for most patients. It is the best performer at ~27% at the label dose but has only ~0.7M users because of cost and tolerability. Survodutide received a complete response letter in Jul 2029 for manufacturing deficiencies at a contract site; Boehringer resubmitted, and a decision is due 2031. Amycretin was filed in Oct 2029, so no decision before Oct 2030; the decision is now expected in H1 2031. MariTide's phase 3 reads out in 2030 and Amgen has not filed, so it is not on the market. Muscle-preserving adjuncts are still in phase 2/3 and none is approved. Global incretin market ~$141B (2029). In the US, the exclusivity cliff of 2031–32 is the subject of every earnings call.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. In the 2029 trial, switching from injectables to Foundayo caused transient nausea in ~20%. Retatrutide's GI rates are highest at top doses.
Elevated with rapid weight loss, and higher with retatrutide.
Absolute risk remains low, with no causal confirmation. The MDL settled in 2029 for undisclosed sums.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Follow-up of the Medicare cohort holds the hip-fracture HR at ~1.3 in users 65+ after more than 2 years. DXA uptake among users 65+ rose to ~45%. Users on the dementia route are the oldest and most fracture-prone group.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning since Jul 2028; CMS DXA code; geriatric guidance pairs dementia-route prescribing with protein and resistance-training plans.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Cohorts are still conflicting; absolute risk very low.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Listed under adverse reactions; no class warning.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new adult signal. Pediatric psychiatric monitoring is now handled under the developmental entry.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Interim data from the FDA-requested postmarketing study (2030, n≈31k) are consistent with the 2027 cohort: clinically meaningful anhedonia in ~6–8% of users versus ~3% of controls, dose-related. A secondary analysis found the rate similar in AUD-indication users, whose low doses offer little protection because they start from a higher baseline of depressive symptoms.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Postmarketing study continues, with the final report due 2031; no labelling. The AUD label lists 'mood changes' among adverse reactions. OPDP sent untitled letters to two telehealth platforms for 'calm' claims.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months. Allocation-driven interruptions in 2029–30 produced a measurable regain wave among Wegovy pill maintenance users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; supports the Foundayo maintenance label and chronic-therapy framing.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron and vitamin D case series continue, including among AUD users with poor baseline nutrition.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years of continuous use; effects of repeated cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About eight years of follow-up now exist, with no new adult organ signal. The effects of cycling on body composition remain the main unknown in adults.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric bone-density and growth PMRs on the adolescent and 6–11 approvals.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: ~9,800 cumulative FDA adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product. During the 2029 allocation, counterfeit 'Wegovy pill' blister packs appeared for the first time; a 2030 FDA lab sample found 40% contained no semaglutide.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Import alert; CBP seizures; India's export licensing tightened. Personal-importation enforcement is still porous.

safety_ledger.effect: Developmental, growth and psychiatric effects in children who started young (height velocity, pubertal timing, restrictive eating)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: A PEDSnet/Sentinel cohort (Jun 2030, n≈41k children who started at ages 9–14, mostly off-label under 12 or at 12–13) found height velocity ~0.6 cm/yr lower than BMI-matched non-users over the first two years. Girls' menarche was a median ~4 months later. Restrictive eating disorder and ARFID diagnoses were 1.9% versus 1.0%. Confounding by intensive weight-focused care is likely, and whether adult height is affected is unknown.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA Drug Safety Communication (Jul 2030) recommending quarterly height and pubertal staging and eating-disorder screening. The 6–11 label already carried a growth PMR, and an FDA label update is under review. AAP issued interim guidance but did not withdraw its pharmacotherapy recommendation.

food_and_beverage.state: About 36% of households have a user. Snack and confectionery volumes are down ~8% from 2025 and sugary drinks ~7%. Dollar sales are roughly flat because of price and premium protein lines. 'GLP-1 friendly' labels have largely disappeared because they no longer differentiate. Packaged-food firms now plan pack sizes around a 'medicated household' as the default shopper in upper-middle-income ZIP codes.

alcohol.state: Since 2025, US spirits volumes are down ~11% and beer ~6%. The AUD approval and ASAM endorsement moved heavy-drinker treatment into primary care. Because the heaviest ~10% of drinkers account for over half of volume, the effect is concentrated. Brown-Forman and Diageo have consolidated more US capacity. Non-alcoholic and 'one-pour' premium lines are the growth segments, and Wisconsin and Ohio taverns report the steepest declines.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat to slightly up. The small plate is now the default portion at casual chains, and 'full portion' is the upcharge. Wedding and event caterers quote for 60% plate consumption. Bar revenue at casual-dining chains is down, while non-alcoholic cocktail attach rates are up.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists are still shrinking but more slowly. The 2029 allocation-driven regain wave lifted stretch and size-range basics. Children's 'husky' sizing lines are being cut back.

fitness.state: Strength training and body-composition scanning are still growing, supported by the bone warning and the dementia-route pairing with resistance training. Youth strength programmes are marketed to parents of medicated children.

insurance.state: Payer structure is unchanged: 43% of employers cover weight management, coverage concentrates on diabetes, cardiovascular and dementia codes, and premium differentials of up to 30% are tied to adherence. Pharmacy trend was ~+10% in 2029 because of the price rise. PBMs steered members to Foundayo during the allocation. Medicare actuaries track the dementia route, now ~$8B annualised.

pharma.state: Lilly gained share as the small-molecule pill avoided the peptide bottleneck. Novo is rebuilding API capacity and has absorbed the Clayton warning letter. US net prices rose in 2029. Ex-US volume is generic-driven. Both firms are positioning for the 2031–32 exclusivity cliff with retatrutide, amycretin and orals.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Among college-educated 35–60-year-olds, being lean says nothing any more, and visible weight now reads as a choice or a lapse that invites a question. In Plano, Texas, and similar affluent suburbs, 'Are you off?' is asked the way 'Are you still drinking?' once was. After the 2029 allocation, a regained body sometimes just meant your pharmacy ran out.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The two tiers persist. Insured and cash-paying users take branded orals with DXA scans, while lower-income users take pricier, more often counterfeit mail-order product, or nothing. The bottom third's rate rose only 2.5 points. Upper-income parents now face the pediatric growth signal; some quietly pause their children's use over the summer, which is a new form of cycling.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals have settled smaller. In medicated households, the family dinner is often one hungry child and two adults who aren't. The 'Bread Alone' fasting network claims ~500 congregations. Hosting advice now assumes most adult guests are on something.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Several dating apps dropped the 'on/off' tag in 2029 because users treated 'on' as the default and 'off' as a disclosure. Desire mismatch remains a common presenting issue in therapy. The AUD indication added a new kind of couple, one sober by pill and one not.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite and craving are now spoken of as one thing, and both are treatable. The counter-movement is smaller and more defensive: the Unmuted collective, church fasting networks, and fat-acceptance and 'natural' groups are explaining themselves rather than setting terms.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Measured clinically meaningful anhedonia in ~6–8% of users versus ~3% of controls (2030 interim postmarketing data). A much larger share report a mild 'quiet' that is now what many people buy the drug for.
interior_life.framing: Telehealth platforms frame it as a product: 'quiet', 'calm', 'craving-free'. The AUD approval gave them on-label language about craving to build on, and lifestyle subscriptions extend it to people without AUD. Clinicians call it a side effect. Employers still call it steadiness. Unmuted still calls it sedation.
interior_life.effect_on_work: About 3.4M employees are in adherence-verified tracks. Separately, ~1.5M cash users subscribe to 'focus' or 'calm' low-dose plans marketed to sales, trading and tech workers as a replacement for evening drinking and impulse spending. Two EEOC ADA charges are still pending.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Sportsbook handle per identifiable user is down further. 'Quiet bars' serving zero-proof drinks have opened in Austin and Denver. The Unmuted collective's 'off nights' now travel to Chicago and Oakland. The 'flat' fiction wave has a parody genre. Stand-up about 'the craving' has become a cliché.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Couples synchronise dosing, and anniversary drug holidays are common. Sex therapists report AUD-indication couples renegotiating relationships that were organised around drinking together.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Coalition politics have stalled rather than advanced. California's adherence-premium bill died in committee in 2029, and Illinois's ban is still the only one. No measurable effect on turnout or mood. AUD-route users are a quiet constituency that defends the drug's price, not its culture.

state.regulatory_posture: Pro-speed on approvals: under-12 injectable, AUD oral, retatrutide and the Foundayo maintenance label all came in this window. The FDA was reactive on supply, issuing the Clayton warning letter without declaring a class shortage, which kept compounding closed. OPDP sent untitled letters to telehealth 'calm' marketers. The pediatric response came as a Drug Safety Communication rather than a label action, so far.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: No new mandate, subsidy or programme. TrumpRx continues. The 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing 30% adherence-tied premium differentials stands unchanged. No new state laws.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Unchanged in structure: PBM fill data and app-linked logs feed wellness vendors; five state employee plans and two Medicaid programmes condition coverage on adherence. AUD-route prescriptions sit under ordinary pharmacy privacy, not 42 CFR Part 2, a gap advocates have flagged.
state.workforce_or_military: The Army's oral pilot for recruits continues. Trucking firms now encourage on-label AUD use; DOT has still not ruled. TRICARE is unchanged.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Oral parity turned peptide API into the strategic chokepoint. Novo is expanding Kalundborg and Clayton. Chinese API supplies most global generic makers. India tightened export licensing after the US contamination case. US–India talks still cover mail-order enforcement. The ~30× US–India price gap is a standing Danish and US campaign issue.

FDA adds weight maintenance after tirzepatide induction to Foundayo's label after a switch trial shows patients kept nearly all their loss; PBMs move allocation-hit patients to the pill

open_tensions: Six months separate the FDA's approval of semaglutide for 6–11-year-olds from its warning about slower growth and more eating disorders in children who started young. The label update and adult-height data are both pending, and upper-income parents are improvising summer drug holidays.

Telehealth sells 'quiet' as a feature on the back of the AUD indication while the FDA's own postmarketing study keeps finding anhedonia in a minority. The final report is due in 2031, and employers still tie premiums to continuous use.

Oral parity made peptide API the bottleneck. One plant's warning letter raised prices for millions and pushed some users into a gray market now selling counterfeit pills, with the 2031–32 US exclusivity cliff approaching.
Medicare's dementia route (~$8B a year) sends the drug to the oldest, most fracture-prone users, still with no weight benefit and no settled evidence on cognition.

prose.headline: Off It? Explain Yourself. The pill went mainstream, the price went up, and now the kids are on it
prose.world_in_600_words:
By the end of 2030 about one American adult in five is taking an incretin, roughly fifty-three million people, and more than one in four has tried one. Most of them take a pill. Last year the FDA let Lilly's small-molecule Foundayo be used to hold weight lost on Zepbound, after a trial in which switchers kept nearly all of it. That made the weekly pen a starting tool and the daily tablet the way people stay on. Nearly six in ten users now take something by mouth.

The pill had a cost nobody priced in. Oral semaglutide uses about seventy times as much peptide as the injection, so when the FDA halted lots at Novo's Clayton, North Carolina plant in May 2029, the Wegovy pill went on allocation for eleven months. The maintenance price on the government's TrumpRx channel rose from $299 to $399, and injectables followed. The $149 starter price stayed, and so did the $1,349 list price nobody pays. People cycled off, regained, and came back on Foundayo, which is a small molecule that doesn't need peptide. Lilly's share rose. Mail-order Indian vials, which had cost less than a takeout lunch, now cost more than two, and for the first time counterfeit blister packs appeared.

Who pays has not changed. Forty-three percent of employers cover weight loss, many only through adherence-verified metabolic tracks, and the federal rule allowing a thirty percent premium differential is unchanged. Medicare still has no weight benefit. It pays through the side doors of diabetes, the heart, the kidneys and, since 2028, dementia risk, a route that now carries about 1.4 million of the oldest and most fracture-prone beneficiaries. California's bill against adherence-tied premiums died in committee. Illinois still stands alone.

Growth came through two new doors. In March the FDA approved oral semaglutide for alcohol use disorder, and the addiction medicine society made it first-line. Heavy drinkers, who buy most of the country's liquor, started getting the pill in primary care, and spirits volumes are now about eleven percent below 2025. Telehealth platforms followed within weeks with subscriptions promising to make cravings go quiet. They sell them to people with no diagnosis at all: traders, salespeople, anyone who wants evenings without the second drink or the cart full of things. Two of those platforms received FDA untitled letters, and the ads changed their adjectives.

The other door opened in January, when injectable semaglutide was approved for children aged six to eleven. In July the FDA published a cohort of forty-one thousand children who had started at nine to fourteen. It found growth slowed by about six-tenths of a centimetre a year, menarche about four months later in girls, and eating-disorder diagnoses nearly doubled. The agency recommended quarterly height checks and eating-disorder screening. A label change is under review, and nobody yet knows whether adult height is affected. Pediatricians kept prescribing and started measuring. In Plano, parents compare notes on summer breaks from the drug.

The culture moved in the other direction from the safety news. Being on it is unremarkable among educated adults in their forties and fifties. Being visibly heavy, or drinking hard, now prompts a polite question. Dating apps dropped the on-or-off tag because 'off' had become the disclosure. Caterers quote for plates that come back sixty percent eaten. The Unmuted collective still holds its off nights, now in Chicago and Oakland, and the church fasting network has grown, but both sound defensive now.

The ledger is unchanged where it was settled. Hip fractures run higher in long-term users over sixty-five. A minority of users lose pleasure in a way the FDA's own study can measure. Regain follows stopping. From the outside the country looks calmer, thinner and more sober, and most of that is true. The children's growth charts are the part nobody can read yet.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Keisha Monroe takes her pill standing at the counter at 6:10, with four ounces of water as the box says. It's Foundayo, $349 this month on LillyDirect. She switched last summer when the Wegovy pharmacy kept saying next week. The dental office where she cleans teeth doesn't cover it. Nobody's does, she says, which isn't true.

On the bus into Columbus an ad shows a man holding a sparkling water. QUIET THE POUR, it says. Ask about once-daily treatment. She thinks of her brother-in-law and doesn't text her sister.

At lunch the new assistant eats a whole burrito. Dr. Pham's hygienist asks, kindly, whether she's 'not on anything yet.' The girl says her mom says it's expensive. Everybody nods.

Keisha eats half a turkey wrap and puts the other half in the fridge with her name on it. It'll be there Friday.

At home Darnell is making spaghetti, a full box, because their son Jalen is ten and always hungry, and because Darnell is off. He stopped in March. He says the quiet felt like Sunday all week. She hasn't asked again.

After dinner she stands Jalen against the pantry doorframe, flattens a book on his hair, and draws a pencil line. The pediatrician mentioned the shot in January. Then in July there was the thing on the news about kids growing slower. The pediatrician's office sent a letter: no changes needed, keep measuring.

The line is a quarter inch above April's.

'Did I grow?' he asks.

'You grew,' she says. She takes a photo of it anyway and saves it to a folder.
